learn.title: Learn about money
learn.lead: Short lessons on the numbers in your own account. You climb one camp at a time, from first steps to the summit.
learn.introBody: 7 questions, about 2 minutes. Answer right and the next one is a little harder; get it wrong and it is a little easier. At the end we know which camp to start you at. It is not a grade and nobody else sees it.
learn.summit: All five camps are behind you. You can redo any lesson any time.

1.name: First steps
1.about: Income, spending and what is left at the end of the month.

2.name: Your budget
2.about: Needs, wants and a fund for the unexpected.

3.name: Saving
3.about: Interest, tax on interest and inflation.

4.name: Credit without traps
4.about: APR, credit cards and what a loan really costs.

5.name: The long run
5.about: Risk, horizon, diversification and your pension.

lesson.locked: This lesson opens once you finish “{name}”.

a.0: the amount that actually lands in your account
a.1: the salary in your contract, before taxes
a.2: your salary plus the year's bonuses

q1.why: Net is what is left after income tax and contributions. It is what you budget with.

q2.q: You earned 3,000 RON this month and spent 3,400 RON. What happened?

a.1: You spent 400 RON more than you earned

q2.why: The extra 400 RON came from savings or from debt.

q3.q: Which of these is a fixed cost?
q3.why: Rent is the same every month. You can adjust the others.

q4.q: The 50/30/20 rule splits your income into…
q4.why: 50% for needs, 30% for wants, 20% for savings. A starting point, not a law.

q5.why: 3–6 months of essentials get you through a month without income or a big repair.

q6.q: Where do you keep your emergency fund?

a.2: In a savings account you can take it out of quickly

q6.why: In an emergency you need the money now, and it should not depend on the stock market.

q7.q: You have 1,000 RON at 5% interest a year. After one year, before tax, you have…
q7.why: 5% of 1,000 RON is 50 RON of interest in a year.

q8.q: Inflation is 6% and your savings earn 4%. The buying power of your money…
q8.why: Prices rise by 6%, your money only by 4%: the same amount buys less.

q9.q: In Romania, money in bank accounts is guaranteed by the Deposit Guarantee Fund up to…

a.1: 100,000 EUR per person, at each bank

q9.why: The fund (FGDB) guarantees up to the equivalent of 100,000 EUR per depositor at each bank.

q10.q: Which number shows the total cost of a loan, fees included?
q10.why: APR adds interest and fees together, so it is the right number to compare loans.

q11.q: You pay only the minimum on your credit card, month after month. What happens?

a.0: You pay interest on the rest, and the debt shrinks slowly
a.1: You pay no interest at all
a.2: The debt is wiped after three months

q11.why: The minimum avoids penalties, but the rest stays as debt that earns interest.

q12.q: Two 10,000 RON loans over 5 years: one with low interest, one with high interest. The monthly payment is higher for…
q12.why: Same amount and term: higher interest means higher payments and a higher total cost.

a.0: spreading your money across several different investments
a.1: putting everything in the investment that grew most

q13.why: If one investment falls, the others can make up for it. The risk is shared.

q14.q: For a goal 30 years away, like retirement, generally…

a.2: you can take more risk, because you have time to ride out falls

q14.why: Over the long run, falls along the way have time to recover. Over the short run, they do not.

a.1: optional and deductible up to the equivalent of 400 EUR a year
a.2: withdrawable any time, at no cost

q15.why: You choose Pillar III. Contributions lower your income tax up to 400 EUR a year, and the money stays until retirement.

net.title: Gross and net

0.title: Two salaries
0.body: Gross is the amount in your contract. Contributions and income tax come out of it, and what is left, net, lands in your account.

1.title: Budgets start from net
1.body: Plan only with money you actually receive. Gross pay and future bonuses do not count.

net.money: Your net salary in Atlas is {net}. That is what you work with this month.

check.q: You build your monthly budget starting from…

a.2: the salary you will have next year

check.why: Net is what reaches your account; the rest is money you never hold.

fixed.title: Fixed and variable costs

0.title: Fixed and variable
0.body: Fixed costs are the same every month: rent, utilities, subscriptions. Variable ones change: eating out, clothes, going out.

1.title: Where you have control
1.body: You rarely change the fixed ones. The variable ones you can adjust week by week, and that is where the difference shows.

fixed.money: Your fixed costs are {essentials} a month. That leaves {rest} for everything else.

check.q: Which one is a variable cost?
check.why: Food orders change from month to month; rent and the pass are fixed.

rule.title: The 50/30/20 rule

0.title: A simple split
0.body: A starting point: 50% of income for needs, 30% for wants and 20% for savings.

1.title: Not a law
1.body: If rent is high, needs go above 50%. Then you trim the wants, you do not drop the savings.

rule.money: On {net}: needs {n50}, wants {n30}, savings {n20}. Your fixed costs are already {essentials}, that is {pct}% of your salary.

check.q: With 4,000 RON net, how much goes to savings under the 50/30/20 rule?

rule.apply: Follow the month's pace in Ritm

emergency.title: The emergency fund

0.title: Money for the unexpected
0.body: A repair, a trip to the doctor, a month without income. The emergency fund is there so you do not borrow then.

1.title: How much and where
1.body: The usual target is 3–6 months of basic costs, in a savings account you can take it out of quickly.

emergency.money: For you, 3 months of basic costs is {e3}. Right now you have {savings} in savings.

check.q: Where do you keep your emergency fund?

a.0: In a savings account, easy to reach

check.why: In an emergency you need the money now, and it should not depend on the stock market.

interest.title: Interest

0.title: How interest works
0.body: The bank pays you interest for money you keep with it. At 4% a year, 1,000 RON earns 40 RON in a year.

1.title: Tax on interest
1.body: In Romania, 10% tax is taken from interest. Of the 40 RON, you keep 36 RON.

interest.moneyHave: {amount} in savings, kept for a year at {rate}% a year, would earn about {interest} after tax.
interest.moneyIf: If you put {amount} in savings for a year at {rate}% a year, you would get about {interest} after tax.

check.q: 1,000 RON at 5% a year. How much interest do you get in a year, before tax?

0.title: Prices go up
0.body: When prices rise, the same money buys less. With 5% inflation a year, a basket that costs 100 RON today costs 105 RON a year from now.

1.title: Interest and inflation
1.body: If interest is lower than inflation, your money loses buying power even while the amount in your account grows.

check.q: Inflation is 6%, interest is 4%. The buying power of your savings…
check.why: Prices rise by 6%, your money only by 4%.

apr.title: APR, the real cost of a loan

0.title: What APR is
0.body: The annual percentage rate puts interest and fees together in one percentage. It is the number you compare between loans.

1.title: Compare fairly
1.body: Two loans with the same interest rate can have different APRs because of fees. Look at the total amount to repay too.

check.q: Which number do you use to compare two loans?
check.why: APR includes the fees too, so it shows the real cost.

0.title: The minimum payment
0.body: On a credit card you can pay just a minimum. The rest stays as debt and earns interest, usually a lot.

1.title: The grace period
1.body: If you pay everything by the due date, you usually pay no interest on purchases.

check.q: You pay only the minimum on your credit card, month after month. What happens?

a.0: You pay interest, and the debt shrinks slowly

check.why: The minimum keeps penalties away, but not interest.

0.title: Time matters
0.body: The more time you have before you need the money, the easier it is to ride out the falls along the way.

1.title: Do not put it all in one place
1.body: Diversifying means spreading money across several investments, so one fall does not hit everything.

check.q: For a goal 30 years away, generally…
check.why: Over the long run, falls have time to recover.

pillar3.title: Pillar III

0.title: The pension pillars
0.body: Pillar I is the state pension. Pillar II goes, for most young employees, to a private fund. Pillar III is optional: you choose it.

1.title: The deduction
1.body: Pillar III contributions lower your income tax, up to 400 EUR a year. The money stays invested until retirement.

pillar3.money: If you put {amount} a year into Pillar III, your income tax would go down by up to {tax}. Funds can be compared on the ASF website; Atlas Pensii is Atlas's own fund.

a.0: optional, with a deduction of up to 400 EUR a year
a.2: withdrawable any time, at no cost

check.why: You choose it, and contributions are deductible up to 400 EUR a year.
